name: Neurofibromatosis Type 1

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: NIH Revised Diagnostic Criteria for NF1 (2021 Update)

criteria.description: >= 6 cafe-au-lait macules (>5 mm in prepubertal, >15 mm in postpubertal individuals)
>= 2 neurofibromas of any type OR 1 plexiform neurofibroma
Freckling in axillary or inguinal region (Crowe sign)
>= 2 Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas) or >= 2 choroidal abnormalities
A distinctive osseous lesion (sphenoid dysplasia, anterolateral tibial bowing, long bone pseudarthrosis)
A heterozygous pathogenic NF1 variant with variant allele fraction >= 50% in apparently normal tissue
A parent meeting the above NF1 diagnostic criteria (in the presence of one of the above criteria in the child)

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Two or more of the above criteria (without a parent with NF1), OR one of the above criteria plus a first-degree relative with NF1
diagnosticCriteria.notes: NF1 is one of the most common autosomal dominant genetic disorders. ~50% are de novo mutations. Complete penetrance by age 8 years. Expression is highly variable, even within families.

pathognomonic.notes: Uniformly hyperpigmented, flat, well-demarcated macules; often first sign
Melanocytic hamartomas on slit-lamp exam; age-dependent (rare before age 3, >90% by adulthood)

common.notes: Soft, fleshy tumors that increase in number with age and during pregnancy
IQ usually normal range but ~50% have learning disabilities
Diffuse, often congenital, involving nerve branches; can cause significant disfigurement

occasional.notes: Usually low-grade pilocytic astrocytoma; majority in first decade of life

occasional.symptomName: Hypertension (essential or from renal artery stenosis/pheochromocytoma)

rare.notes: Lifetime risk 8-13%; most serious complication; often arises from plexiform neurofibroma

rare.symptomName: Breast cancer (increased risk in young women)

laboratory: Complete blood count if JMML suspected in children
imaging: MRI brain and orbits for optic pathway gliomas
Whole-body MRI for plexiform neurofibroma surveillance
PET/CT if MPNST suspected (FDG-avid compared to benign neurofibromas)
genetic: Autosomal dominant with complete penetrance but variable expressivity
Large gene with high mutation rate
other: OCT (optical coherence tomography) for choroidal abnormalities

distinguishingFeatures: Cafe-au-lait macules and freckling but NO neurofibromas
No optic gliomas or bone abnormalities
Cafe-au-lait macules with irregular 'coast of Maine' borders
Cafe-au-lait macules present but associated with childhood cancers
Biallelic MMR gene mutations (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2)
Brain tumors and GI cancers in childhood

redFlags: Rapidly growing or painful plexiform neurofibroma (concern for MPNST transformation)
New-onset persistent pain or neurological deficit associated with neurofibroma
Unexplained hypertension (screen for renal artery stenosis or pheochromocytoma)
Progressive visual loss (optic pathway glioma expansion)
Tibial bowing in infancy (risk of pseudarthrosis)
references: Legius E, et al. Revised diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 1 and Legius syndrome: an international consensus recommendation. Genet Med. 2021;23(8):1506-1513.
Gutmann DH, et al. Neurofibromatosis type 1. Nat Rev Dis Primers. 2017;3:17004.
Ferner RE, et al. Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of individuals with neurofibromatosis 1. J Med Genet. 2007;44(2):81-88.
Evans DG, et al. Birth incidence and prevalence of tumor-prone syndromes: estimates from a UK family genetic register service. Am J Med Genet A. 2010;152A(2):327-332.
